rationale: Symmetry is common in organisms, but it is not in general a minimal-energy equilibrium like a liquid film: body symmetry is set by developmental patterning in open, far-from-equilibrium systems, and stable asymmetries (flatfishes, fiddler-crab claws, spiral shells, sponges) occur without any failure of mechanical stability. The amoeba’s shifting outline is continual cytoskeletal remodeling, not a special absence of equilibrium.

For equal pressure jump and uniform tension, Laplace’s relation makes the end a sphere of radius twice the cylinder’s, so the cap is a 60° cone of height (2−√3) times the cylinder radius, about 0.27R and a little over one-eighth of the diameter. Those proportions are only sometimes suggested by the free ends of Spirogyra, whose cellulose cross-walls are often nearly plane and are not isotropic fluid films.

Cortical tension shapes some naked cells, but unicellular form and asymmetry generally follow cell walls, pellicles, and cytoskeletal pattern, from bacterial peptidoglycan to diatom shells and ciliate cortices, rather than local surface-tension differences on a fluid surface.

A deflecting bias of fixed compass direction bends a growing axis toward an asymptote and does not keep turning it into a spiral, so that kinematic claim holds. A spiral is not produced only by an intrinsic force that turns with growth, and the snail shell coils by asymmetric accretion at the mantle edge, not by the columellar muscle, which retracts the body into the shell.

Related fishes often do differ by a smooth whole-body deformation, and geometric morphometrics shows that much shape change is integrated. That does not replace selection on separately varying parts: selection on correlated, developmentally modular variation produces both global warps and local change, and the existence of a coordinate map is not a proof of one comprehensive law of growth.

One smooth grid deformation carries the porcupinefish outline roughly onto the ocean sunfish and leaves the head relatively less altered, in line with their shared tetraodontiform plan. It does not cover every external difference—spines versus the sunfish’s spineless truncated clavus, fin structure, and other local traits sit outside a single outline warp—and the published figure is a schematic fit.
